posts.excerpt: Some spiral galaxies look heavier or more elongated on one side than the other. Why galaxies get lopsided is not fully understood. In a new study, astronomers combined measurements of galaxies from 37 studies to create a big catalog and analyzed it to check for lopsidedness and its cause. posts.title: A Bedroom with an Extra Window
posts.excerpt: Frederik van Eeden woke to the sound of a luggage box being blown along the landing. It was July 1906, and he was staying at Langen Schwalbach after a tiring day. The tremendous bumping ought to have brought the house to life. Instead, it alerted him to something he had learned to recognise. He was apparently awake in his bedroom, but the night had taken a familiar turn. On another apparent awakening he counted three windows in the room. He knew there should be two. When he deliberately woke himself, the extra window was gone. By his account, the house had been quiet all night.

posts.title: From broken circuits to growing graphite: A new role for electromigration
posts.excerpt: Inside electronic devices, electric current can gradually displace atoms within tiny metal connections, creating gaps or unwanted accumulations that eventually cause circuits to fail. This phenomenon, known as electromigration, has long been regarded as a reliability problem that engineers must work to prevent. Yet the ability of an electric current to move atoms also raises the possibility of putting that movement to constructive use, directing atoms through a material rather than allowing them to migrate uncontrollably.

posts.title: Successful high-purity synthesis of the challenging-to-produce cerium orthoferrite!
posts.excerpt: A research team including scientists from Ehime University successfully synthesized high-purity CeFeO3, a difficult-to-produce cerium–iron mixed oxide, using hydrogen reduction. posts.title: As Americans gather for Thanksgiving, a centuries‑old Sikh tradition offers an expansive vision of hospitality
posts.excerpt: On Sundays at Gurdwara Guru Nanaksar in Chapin, South Carolina, diners sit in rows on the floor while volunteers walk along each row carrying pots and trays of food. They pause to offer each person a spoonful of dal, a dish made with lentils, or a serving of vegetables. When the roti—a kind of flatbread—comes around, diners hold out both hands, palms up. A volunteer places the bread directly into their hands. This is "langar," the free communal meal served at Sikh houses of worship around the world.

posts.title: Miniaturization found at the origin of amphibians opens new ecological territory
posts.excerpt: Frogs, salamanders and caecilians—the three groups of living amphibians—together number more than 9,000 species. On average, they are the smallest of all four-limbed vertebrates, and some are extremely small: Brachycephalus toads measure less than 7 millimeters (0.28 inches) from snout to vent. Their ancient relatives were very different animals. Most temnospondyls, the extinct group from which modern amphibians (lissamphibians) arose, were aquatic or semiaquatic predators 1 to 5 meters (3.3 to 16.4 feet) long.

posts.title: How does ocean carbon sequestration change under different glacial conditions?
posts.excerpt: Over the past 800,000 years, Earth's history has been marked by dramatic shifts in climate, swinging from warm periods to cold, when large ice sheets covered much of the Northern Hemisphere and sea ice greatly expanded. The transition between the two climates is paced by the Earth's orbit with respect to the sun, but changes in the amount of carbon dioxide (CO2), a greenhouse gas, also affect global temperatures. By understanding how CO2 is exchanged between the atmosphere and the ocean, scientists hope to apply that knowledge to future climate scenarios.

posts.excerpt: NASA's Curiosity rover has been collecting data about Mars' thin, carbon dioxide–rich atmosphere since 2012. What they found suggests a process involving water either attached to soil grains or in extremely thin, liquid-like films at the surface.

posts.title: Tam Thien Cave System (Tam Thiên Động) in Quy Nhon Dong, Vietnam
posts.excerpt:
Hidden along the rugged coastline near the famous Ky Co beach in Nhon Ly fishing village, Tam Thien Cave is an extraordinary system of three interconnected sea caves that remains largely unknown to most travelers.

posts.title: Nanogap architecture could help integrate quantum light sources onto chips
posts.excerpt: Quantum light sources that emit light with special quantum properties, such as single photons, are critical for quantum photonic technologies, including quantum communication, computing and sensing. In this regard, monolayer tungsten diselenide (WSe₂), a two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor material, hosts localized emissive states that enable light emission with sharp or narrow line widths, meaning that the emitted light has a narrow range of photon energies. This sharp luminescence makes this material a promising candidate for implementing on-chip quantum light sources.

posts.title: The color of uniformity: Far-red light effects on plant growth
posts.excerpt: Ever wandered through a field of plants and observed how their heights are relatively uniform? In nature, this is partly due to plants' ability to sense their neighbors through light receptors and shade-avoidance responses. When a lower ratio of red to far-red (FR) light is detected due to the presence of neighboring plants, plants elongate their stems to compete for light.

posts.title: New observations challenge evidence for an 'outsize' black hole in the early universe
posts.excerpt: A recent reanalysis of the outsize black hole galaxy UHZ1 using existing X-ray data and new infrared observations challenges a previous groundbreaking claim. Three years ago, this galaxy made news for hosting an unusually massive and heavily dust-obscured black hole formed through direct collapse. Led by Fan Zou of the University of Michigan, the new study reports no signs of hidden black hole activity. The paper, published in The Astrophysical Journal on Oct. 14, suggests UHZ1 could be a low-mass, metal-poor, star-forming galaxy.

posts.title: What Crossed Route 542 in the Rain?
posts.excerpt: Keyara Klawitter was driving through the New Jersey Pine Barrens on 11 October when her high beams picked out something stepping into Route 542. She was coming around the bend near Loveland Lane, outside New Gretna. The figure entered from her right. She braked. By the time it reached the other side, she had seen enough to pick out long arms, hands she thought looked human and a coat of black fur that shone in the headlights. She remembered the fur looking soaked. Her children slept through it in the back seat.

posts.excerpt: The advance of urbanization in the São Paulo Metropolitan Area in Brazil is causing the collapse of food webs in local streams. posts.excerpt: Since 2022, astronomers have been puzzling over a new kind of cosmic object called long-period radio transients. These are objects that emit bright flashes of radio waves into space every few minutes to every few hours. Some have been traced back to binary systems consisting of a small, dim, cool star called a red dwarf in orbit with a stellar remnant called a white dwarf.

posts.excerpt: Lake Baikal in Siberia holds around 20% of the world's surface freshwater, making it the most voluminous freshwater lake (Lake Superior on the United States–Canada border is the largest by surface area). This makes the lake one of the most important environments for biodiversity—in fact, it was designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1996 because of this. Yet it has shown considerable decline over the last century, with aridification spreading across East Asia.
